name: Scotland
note: In Scotland the doctor who attended the deceased must issue a medical certificate of cause of death within seven days, normally sent electronically by the Health Board to the Registrar General, and a sample of certificates is randomly reviewed by medical reviewers of Healthcare Improvement Scotland before registration; suspicious deaths go to the procurator fiscal. A relative, person present, executor or occupier (or the funeral director on their behalf) must register the death within eight days, in person or remotely as the Registrar General directs, and receives a free certificate of registration that is needed before burial or cremation. National Records of Scotland passes deaths to DWP and keeps the NHS Central Register; Tell Us Once covers the other UK bodies. Uniquely in the UK, the Registrar General may, for a fee, give notice of a registered death to a third party who applies, though this is not a bulk verification service.

steps.title: Death is verified by a doctor, nurse or paramedic
steps.who: A registered medical practitioner, or in practice a nurse or paramedic under professional guidance.
steps.summary: No statutory rule on verification of death was found; recorded as unverified.

steps.title: Doctor reports a sudden, suspicious or unexplained death to the procurator fiscal
steps.who: The doctor (or police) aware of the death; the procurator fiscal (COPFS) investigates. Scotland has no coroner.
steps.trigger: A death that is sudden, suspicious, accidental, unexplained or otherwise reportable under Crown Office guidance.
steps.summary: Reporting to the procurator fiscal rests on Crown Office guidance rather than statute; the COPFS and gov.scot pages were not reachable, so this step is unverified.

steps.title: Attending doctor issues the medical certificate of cause of death
steps.who: The registered medical practitioner who attended the deceased during the last illness, or, if none can, any medical practitioner able to do so.

deadline.text: within seven days after the death (or other prescribed period of at least two days)

steps.summary: The certificate goes to a qualified informant or directly to a district registrar.

steps.title: Health Board sends death particulars to the Registrar General
steps.who: Each Health Board, for every death in its area; the Registrar General (National Records of Scotland) makes them available to every district registrar.
steps.summary: The statutory basis for the electronic MCCD: certificate particulars flow from the NHS to the Registrar General and on to any registrar, so the informant can register anywhere in Scotland.

steps.title: Random and targeted review of certificates by medical reviewers
steps.who: The Registrar General refers randomly selected certificates (and descriptions requested by medical reviewers); a district registrar may also refer one. Reviewers act for Healthcare Improvement Scotland.
steps.summary: Unlike England and Wales, only a sample of certificates is reviewed before registration. Certificates of deaths being investigated by the procurator fiscal are excluded.

steps.title: Medical reviewer reports suspected criminality to the procurator fiscal
steps.who: A medical reviewer or the senior medical reviewer.
steps.trigger: Suspicion of criminality arising from a review.
steps.summary: The reviewer must report and then follow the procurator fiscal's directions.

steps.title: Interested person may ask for a review of the certificate
steps.who: A qualified informant, a health professional or carer involved in the deceased's care, the funeral director, or another interested person.

deadline.text: within three years of the date of death

steps.summary: A medical reviewer must review the certificate unless the application is rejected (e.g. as vexatious) and notifies the Registrar General.

steps.title: Informant registers the death with any district registrar
steps.who: Any relative, any person present at the death, the executor or legal representative, the occupier of the premises, or failing them anyone with knowledge of the particulars. One informant discharges the others.
steps.trigger: The death (or finding of the body).

deadline.text: within eight days from the date of the death (or the finding of the body)

steps.summary: Information is given by attending the registration office and attesting the death registration form, or in another manner permitted by a direction of the registrar or the Registrar General (remote registration). Failure to give the information, where it is not given, is an offence.

steps.title: Funeral director may register the death on the family's behalf
steps.who: The funeral director responsible for arranging the funeral.

deadline.text: within eight days from the date of the death

steps.summary: Since 2022 the funeral director giving the information discharges every informant's duty.

steps.title: Registrar and procurator fiscal exchange information about reportable deaths
steps.who: District registrar (on the Registrar General's instructions) and the procurator fiscal.
steps.trigger: A death the registrar must intimate to the procurator fiscal under the Registrar General's directions.
steps.summary: The procurator fiscal confirms or corrects the particulars to the Registrar General after a precognition; where the fiscal learns of such a death elsewhere, it notifies the registrar.

steps.title: Registrar issues a free certificate of registration, required for burial or cremation
steps.who: The district registrar gives it to the informant, for the person in charge of the place of interment or cremation.
steps.summary: Interring or cremating a body without the specified certificates is an offence by the person in charge of the burial ground or crematorium.

steps.title: Anyone may obtain an extract of the death entry
steps.localName: extract of an entry in the register of deaths
steps.who: Any person who pays the fee, from a district registrar or the Registrar General.
steps.summary: Death extracts are open: any person may search the indexes and obtain an extract.

steps.title: Registrar General for Scotland sends death particulars to DWP
steps.who: The Registrar General of Births, Deaths and Marriages for Scotland.

deadline.text: as soon as reasonably practicable after registration (where the council facilitates the notification service), otherwise as the Secretary of State directs

steps.summary: See uk-national for the UK-wide DWP feed and Tell Us Once.

steps.title: Registrar General updates the NHS Central Register
steps.who: The Registrar General (National Records of Scotland), for Health Boards, Public Health Scotland, the Common Services Agency and local authorities.
steps.trigger: Registration of a death in the registers transmitted to the Registrar General.
steps.summary: The Registrar General may keep a central register of individuals built from the birth and death registers, used by health and local authorities.

steps.title: Electoral registration officer may inspect registrars' records
steps.summary: Electoral registration officers may inspect and copy records kept by registrars of births, deaths and marriages.

steps.title: Informant may ask the Registrar General to notify named persons of the death
steps.who: On application by a qualified informant, in the prescribed form and with a fee, to the Registrar General or any district registrar.
steps.trigger: Registration of the death and the informant's application.
steps.summary: The Registrar General may give notice of the death to persons the informant names (for example a bank or insurer), if it considers it appropriate.

steps.title: A third party may apply to be notified of a registered death
steps.who: Any applicant, in the prescribed form and with a fee.
steps.trigger: The applicant's application; the death must have been registered.
steps.summary: The Registrar General may give the applicant notice of a death in Scotland if appropriate. This is an individual, per-death notification power, not a bulk death file.

registrationDeadlineDays.note: Eight days from the death or the finding of the body (a different period of at least three days may be prescribed).

informantDuty.note: The duty lies equally on any relative, any person present at the death, the executor or legal representative, and the occupier; others only if there is no such person. A funeral director may discharge it for them.

medicalExaminerScrutiny.note: Not every certificate: medical reviewers (Healthcare Improvement Scotland) review a random sample and targeted categories before registration, plus any certificate an interested person asks about.

electronicRegistration.note: Medical certificate particulars go electronically from Health Boards to the Registrar General, and registration may be done remotely under Registrar General directions, but the informant (or funeral director) must still give the information to a registrar and attest the death registration form.

certificateAccess.note: Any person who pays the fee may obtain an extract.

centralPopulationRegister.name: NHS Central Register (Scotland)
centralPopulationRegister.note: A register of individuals kept by the Registrar General from birth and death registrations for health boards and local authorities; it is a health-administration register rather than a general population register.

privateSectorVerification.note: No bulk death data for private bodies, but the Registrar General may notify persons named by the informant (s. 39A) and any third-party applicant of a specific registered death (s. 39B), for a fee.

gaps: Reporting of deaths to the procurator fiscal (Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service guidance) could not be read: www.copfs.gov.uk was blocked by egress policy and www.gov.scot returned an empty HTTP 202 (apparent bot challenge). The doctor-to-fiscal step is unverified.

National Records of Scotland (www.nrscotland.gov.uk and nrscotland.gov.uk), ScotlandsPeople (www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk) and mygov.scot (www.mygov.scot) were blocked, so the operation of s. 39A/39B notices (prescribed forms, fees, whether the service is actually offered) and remote-registration directions could not be confirmed.

Registration of Births, Deaths and Marriages (Scotland) regulations prescribing the forms (death registration form, Form 14) and the Certification of Death (Scotland) Act 2011 regulations on review timescales were not read.
Verification of the fact of death has no statutory basis found; the pronounce step is unverified.
Whether NHSCR is still operated by NRS under s. 57 or has moved to Public Health Scotland was not established.
